scenario: You hear a nuclear detonation occurred 15 miles from your location. You are indoors in a concrete building. The wind is blowing TOWARD you from the direction of the detonation. FEMA guidance says: what is the correct action?

options.text: Evacuate immediately — 15 miles is within the severe fallout zone and you must leave now
Shelter-in-place immediately — go to the center of a middle floor, seal windows/doors, turn off HVAC, and monitor for official guidance within 24 hours
Evacuate perpendicular to the wind — drive crosswind to avoid the fallout plume
Go to the basement for 3-7 days — underground provides the most shielding

explanation: The FEMA/DHS 'Get Inside, Stay Inside, Stay Tuned' guidance: at 15 miles and winds toward you, fallout arrives in approximately 15-30 minutes. You do NOT have time to safely evacuate — you will be caught in the open during peak fallout. Shelter-in-place in a substantial building (concrete, brick) dramatically reduces radiation exposure. Fallout intensity decreases by the Rule of 7: for every 7x increase in time after detonation, radiation reduces by a factor of 10 (7 hours = 90% reduction, 49 hours = 99% reduction). The center of a middle floor is optimal (most mass between you and the exterior). Basement is better than nothing but may not be available. Stay sealed for minimum 24 hours, preferably 48-72, or until official guidance. Do NOT open the building during peak fallout.

scenario: You are indoors in a multi-story office building when a strong earthquake begins. Place these actions in the correct order.

items.text: Drop to your hands and knees right where you are
Cover your head and neck - crawl under a sturdy desk or table if one is close
Hold on until the shaking stops - do not try to run outside while the building is moving
After the shaking stops, check yourself for injuries, then help others
If the building is damaged, leave by the stairs (never the elevator) and move away from the building

explanation: Drop, Cover, and Hold On is the guidance from FEMA Ready.gov, CDC, and the Great ShakeOut. Drop first so the shaking cannot knock you down. Cover your head and neck, under a sturdy table if one is close, because falling and flying objects cause most injuries. Hold on until the shaking ends - people who try to run outside or to another room during shaking are more likely to be hurt. Once it stops, check yourself first, then others. If the building is damaged, get out using the stairs, since elevators may fail, and move away from walls, glass, and power lines. Do not stand in a doorway - in modern buildings it is no stronger than anywhere else. Expect aftershocks and Drop, Cover, Hold On again each time.

scenario: Floodwaters from a nearby river have gone down. Your private water well was underwater during the flood. When is it safe to drink water from the well again?

options.text: As soon as the water looks clear - the flood washed the contaminants away as it drained
After the well has been inspected, shock-chlorinated, flushed, and a lab test shows it is free of bacteria
After running the pump for 30 minutes to flush the floodwater out
Never - a flooded well is ruined and a new one must be drilled

explanation: A flooded well can be contaminated with sewage, farm runoff, fuel, and chemicals that you cannot see or smell. Clear water is not proof it is safe, and running the pump alone does not clean the well casing or the ground around it. Health agencies advise having the well and pump checked (they may also be an electrical hazard), disinfecting it with a shock chlorination using your state or local health department's instructions, flushing it until the chlorine is gone, and then testing it at a certified lab for coliform bacteria and E. coli. Until results come back clean, use bottled or stored water, or boil water if germs are the only concern. Most flooded wells can be restored - drilling a new one is rarely needed.

scenario: You are driving home at night in heavy rain. Ahead, water is flowing across the road. It looks only a few inches deep, and a pickup just drove through it. What should you do?

options.text: Drive through slowly and steadily, like the pickup did
Turn around and find another route
Get out and wade in to check the depth before driving through
Drive through fast so the car does not have time to float

explanation: Turn Around, Don't Drown. More than half of U.S. flood deaths happen in vehicles. About 12 inches (30 cm) of water can float a small car, and 18-24 inches (45-60 cm) of moving water can carry off most vehicles, including SUVs and pickups. At night you cannot judge depth or see whether the road beneath has washed away. Another driver making it across tells you nothing about what is under the water now. Wading in is also dangerous - six inches (15 cm) of fast water can knock you down. Speed makes it worse by throwing up water that can stall the engine and cause loss of control.

scenario: A Tornado Warning is issued while you are driving on an open highway. You see the tornado in the distance and debris is starting to blow across the road. A highway overpass is just ahead. What is the best choice?

options.text: Stop under the overpass and climb up under the girders for shelter
Stop in the traffic lane and stay in the car
Pull off out of traffic; stay buckled with your head below the windows and covered, or lie in a spot clearly lower than the road and cover your head
Speed up and try to outrun the tornado in whatever direction the road goes

explanation: Ready.gov and the NWS say no option in a car is truly safe, but some are less dangerous. Once debris or strong winds reach you, pull out of traffic. Then either stay buckled, get your head below the windows, and cover it - or, if you can get noticeably lower than the roadway, leave the car and lie flat there with your head covered. Never shelter under an overpass: it gives little protection from flying debris, winds can be stronger there, and stopped cars block traffic and rescuers. Driving away only makes sense earlier, when the tornado is far off and you can move at right angles to its path - not when debris is already blowing across the road.

scenario: You are at the beach when the ground shakes hard for almost a minute. When it stops, the ocean starts pulling back fast, exposing sand and rocks far out from shore. No siren has sounded and your phone shows no alert. What do you do?

options.text: Walk out onto the exposed sea floor to look for stranded fish and shells
Wait on the beach for an official tsunami warning before deciding
Get in your car and drive along the coast road to warn others
Leave immediately on foot for high ground or inland, following tsunami route signs

explanation: Strong, long shaking near the coast and the sea suddenly pulling back are both natural tsunami warning signs. A tsunami from a nearby quake can arrive in minutes, before any official alert can reach you, so the shaking itself is the warning. Go right away, on foot if you can, to high ground or inland - roughly 100 feet (30 m) up or 1 mile (1.6 km) inland, or out of the hazard zone. The water will return with great force, so never walk onto an exposed sea floor. Driving along the coast keeps you in the danger zone and can jam roads that others need.

scenario: A wildfire is spreading toward your neighborhood. Officials have not yet ordered your zone to evacuate, but a nearby zone is under an evacuation warning. Put these actions in the best order.

items.text: Turn on alerts and local news and confirm your evacuation zone name
Put go-bags, medicines, pets, and N95s in the car, parked facing out with a full tank
Close windows, vents, and doors (leave them unlocked) and move patio cushions and doormats away from the house
Leave as soon as an order comes - or sooner if you feel unsafe - with headlights on and air on recirculate
Return only after officials give the all-clear, and clean ash with a damp method while wearing an N95

explanation: This follows the Ready, Set, Go! approach. Get information first so you know which alerts apply to you. Then load the car so you can leave in minutes. Closing up the house keeps embers out, and leaving doors unlocked helps firefighters; removing burnable items near the walls cuts ember ignitions. Leave early - waiting to see flames puts you on smoky, jammed roads and pulls crews away from the fire to rescue people. Go home only on the all-clear, and do not dry-sweep ash, which throws fine particles into the air.

scenario: Your soccer team is practicing on an open field. The sky overhead is still mostly blue, but you hear a distant rumble of thunder to the west. The coach wants to finish the last 20 minutes. What is the right call?

options.text: Keep playing until you see lightning or it starts to rain
Stop now, get everyone into a fully enclosed building or hard-topped cars, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder
Move the team under the open-sided picnic shelter by the field
Have everyone crouch low on the field until the storm passes

explanation: When thunder roars, go indoors. If you can hear thunder, you are within striking distance - lightning can hit 10 miles (16 km) or more from the rain, often under clear sky ahead of the storm. Only a fully enclosed building with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped metal vehicle with the windows up, protects you. Picnic shelters, dugouts, and tents do not. Crouching outdoors only slightly lowers risk and is a last resort when no shelter is reachable. Stay sheltered until 30 minutes after the last thunder, and restart the clock each time you hear more.

scenario: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center issues a G4 (severe) geomagnetic storm watch for tomorrow night. A friend says you should unplug every device and wrap your phones and radios in foil because the storm will fry them. What is the most accurate response?

options.text: Your friend is right - a G4 storm acts like an EMP and will destroy personal electronics
Nothing at all can happen; solar storms only make pretty auroras
Personal electronics are not at risk, but a severe storm can strain the power grid and degrade GPS and HF radio, so have normal outage supplies and a non-GPS navigation backup ready
Stay indoors because the storm's radiation is dangerous to people on the ground

explanation: Geomagnetic storms push extra currents through very long conductors like power lines, so the main risks are grid voltage problems, possible outages, degraded satellite navigation (GPS), and fading HF radio - plus satellite problems and extra radiation for high-altitude polar flights. They do not fry phones, radios, or cars the way a nuclear EMP might, so foil wrapping is not needed. Earth's atmosphere protects people on the ground from the radiation. A G4 storm is serious for grid and satellite operators, so the sensible household step is the same as for any outage: water, lights, a radio, a way to charge phones, and a paper map.

scenario: A severe solar storm watch is issued for tomorrow night. Your neighbor says it will 'fry every phone and car like an EMP' and plans to bury his electronics. What is the most accurate view of what a solar storm threatens?

options.text: It will destroy all handheld electronics and stop most cars, just like a nuclear EMP
It mainly threatens long power lines, large grid transformers, satellites, GPS, and radio - not small unplugged devices
It is harmless to everything on the ground and needs no preparation
It mainly causes radiation sickness in people outdoors at night

explanation: A solar storm (geomagnetic disturbance) acts like the slow E3 part of a nuclear EMP: it drives currents in long conductors, which can trip or damage the grid and large transformers, and it disrupts satellites, GPS, and radio. It lacks the fast E1 spike that threatens small electronics, so phones and cars are not 'fried.' It is not harmless - the 1989 storm blacked out much of Quebec for about nine hours - so prepare for a possible outage: fill water, charge batteries, and unplug sensitive gear. It does not cause radiation sickness on the ground.

scenario: News reports a nuclear detonation in a city 30 miles away. You have a box of potassium iodide (KI) tablets in your kit. Officials have not said anything about KI yet. What should you do with the KI?

options.text: Take a double dose now for extra protection before the fallout arrives
Get inside a sturdy building, and take KI only if public health officials tell you to, following the label
Skip shelter, because KI protects your whole body from radiation
Take iodine antiseptic from the first aid kit since it works the same way

explanation: FDA says KI protects only the thyroid from radioactive iodine and should be taken only when public health or emergency officials say so. More than the directed dose adds no protection and can cause serious harm. It does not protect the rest of the body, so getting inside and staying inside at least 24 hours is still the main protection. Iodine antiseptic and iodized salt are not substitutes and can be dangerous.

scenario: A train carrying chlorine derails near your two-story house with a basement. Officials order residents to shelter in place. Which room is the best choice to seal?

options.text: The basement, because underground rooms give the most protection
The attached garage, since you can keep the car running for heat
A large upstairs bathroom with one small window and a water source
The ground-floor living room with large windows so you can watch the cloud

explanation: CDC advises sealing a room on the highest floor possible with few windows and, ideally, a water source. Many toxic gases, including chlorine, are heavier than air and collect in basements and low spots, so the basement is the wrong choice here - even though it is the best spot for radiation. Running a car in a garage risks carbon monoxide poisoning, and big windows are hard to seal.

scenario: The smoke alarm goes off at 2 a.m. and the hallway outside your bedroom smells of smoke. Put these actions in the right order.

items.text: Feel the bedroom door with the back of your hand before opening it
Call 911 from the outside meeting place
Crawl low under the smoke to the nearest safe exit, closing doors behind you
Go to the meeting place in front of the house and count heads

explanation: Alert everyone first, then check the door: if it is hot, use your second way out. Crawl low where the air is cleaner and close doors to slow the fire. Go straight to the meeting place so you can tell who is missing, then call 911 from outside. Never go back in - tell firefighters who is still inside. Calling from inside wastes the seconds you need to escape.

scenario: Your town issued a boil-water notice after a water main break. You live at 2,000 feet. Which plan is correct?

options.text: Boil water for 1 minute at a rolling boil for drinking, cooking, ice, brushing teeth, and baby formula
Boil water for 10 seconds; just reaching a boil kills everything
Run tap water through a fridge filter - that makes it safe to drink
Boiling is unnecessary for brushing teeth or making ice, only for drinking

explanation: CDC and EPA say to bring water to a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes at high altitude - CDC uses 6,500 feet, EPA a lower cutoff, so use 3 minutes above about 5,000 feet). At 2,000 feet, 1 minute is enough. Use safe water for anything you or a baby might swallow, including ice and toothbrushing. Most fridge and pitcher filters are not designed to remove germs, and you should replace them after the notice is lifted.

scenario: You return home after a flood. When you open the front door you smell rotten eggs, and the hallway is dark. What should you do?

options.text: Flip on the hall light to find the source of the smell
Light a candle so you can see the gas meter
Shut off the main gas valve if you can do it safely, open windows, leave, and call the gas company from outside
Turn the gas off, wait 10 minutes, then relight the pilot lights yourself

explanation: A rotten-egg smell means a likely gas leak. CDC says to turn off the main gas valve if possible, open windows, leave right away, and report it from outside. Light switches, phones, and flames can spark an explosion. Do not go back in until the gas company or fire department says it is safe, and let the utility or a licensed professional turn gas back on and relight pilots.

start.scenario: Your car stopped in traffic simultaneously with all other vehicles. Traffic lights are off. Your cell phone is completely dead. Store alarms are going off citywide. Based on these indicators, you suspect an EMP event. You are 12 miles from home with your everyday carry bag. What is your first action?

options.text: Begin the 12-mile walk home immediately — retrieve your family and supplies
Stop, observe the situation for 10-15 minutes, gather information from people around you before committing to an action

observe_first.scenario: After 15 minutes you confirm: no vehicles work, no cell phones work, no radio from anyone nearby. A police officer on foot approaches saying he received no communications before his radio died. This confirms a broad EM event. Do you:

options.text: Begin walking home — 12 miles is a 4-hour walk, daylight is available
Look for a pre-1985 diesel vehicle that may have survived — older vehicles have no solid-state electronics

walk_home.explanation: Walking home is correct when the distance is manageable and daylight is available. 12 miles = approximately 4 hours at a comfortable pace. Key walking-home principles: stay off main roads where possible (less exposure to panicking crowds), carry water and a snack, navigate by landmark/sun/compass rather than GPS. At home: implement 72-hour plan immediately — fill bathtubs, take cash, implement comms plan with out-of-area contact, move critical supplies to a secure location. The first 72 hours are about information gathering and security, not long-term logistics.

find_old_vehicle.explanation: Old diesel vehicles are a legitimate EMP contingency. The challenge: you must find one, the owner must be willing to help you, and fuel availability is uncertain (though mechanical diesel pumps at some stations may still work). This is a viable secondary approach but takes time — weigh the time cost of searching versus the certainty of walking. If you find a working vehicle in 30 minutes, it's worth it. If it takes 2+ hours, you've lost your daylight walking window.

start.scenario: A Category 3 hurricane (sustained winds 111-129 mph) is forecast to make landfall in about 36 hours, and your area is under a Hurricane Watch and a Storm Surge Watch. You live in an older wood-frame house in evacuation zone B, where 4-6 feet of surge is possible. No evacuation order has been issued for your zone yet. What do you do?

options.text: Leave now for a friend's home inland, outside the surge zone
Wait for an official evacuation order - the storm may still turn

evacuate_now.explanation: Leaving early is a sound choice. Storm surge, not wind, causes most hurricane deaths, and a home in a surge zone can flood deeply no matter how well it is built. Going 36 hours ahead lets you beat the traffic and fuel shortages that build as landfall gets closer, and you only need to go far enough inland to get out of the surge and flood zone into a sturdy building - run from the water, hide from the wind. If the storm turns, the cost is a wasted trip. Take your kit, medicines, documents, and pets, and keep following official updates.

wait_mandatory.explanation: Waiting can work if an order comes in time and you can leave right away, but it is risky here. Orders often arrive when roads are already jammed and gas is short, and people with medical needs, pets, children, or no car need more lead time. A Storm Surge Watch means life-threatening flooding is possible in your area. Emergency managers urge people in surge zones to have their plan ready and leave as soon as they are told - or sooner if they need extra time. At minimum, fuel the car and pack now so you can go the moment your zone is called.
